entities.summary:
The Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria is one of the world's oldest Christian churches, tracing its founding to the Evangelist Mark who brought Christianity to Alexandria, Egypt, around 42 CE. The ancient church of Egypt, the Copts maintained their distinct Christian tradition through Roman persecution, the Council of Chalcedon's 451 CE schism, Arab conquest, and centuries of Islam's dominance — making them the world's oldest continuous Christian community in a predominantly Muslim country.

The Coptic Church diverged from Rome and Constantinople at the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) over the nature of Christ. The Copts held that Christ has a single divine-human nature (miaphysitism), while Chalcedon decreed two natures. This 'Monophysite' split — though Copts reject the term — meant Egypt's Christians developed separately from both Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism for 1,600 years.

Egypt's Arab conquest in 640 CE gradually transformed a Christian majority country into a Muslim majority one, but approximately 10-15% of Egypt's population remains Coptic Christian — around 10-15 million people. The Coptic Pope, currently Tawadros II, is the 118th in the lineage from Saint Mark. Coptic Christians have faced periodic persecution, church bombings (2017 Palm Sunday attacks killed 45), and discrimination. Pope Francis and Tawadros II's 2023 joint declaration on baptism ended 1,600 years of division on that sacrament.
